newsitem.title: IRAN: For Iranian voters it's simple -- it's the economy.
newsitem.headline: For Iranian voters it's simple -- it's the economy.

text.p: Iranian voters who go the polls to chose a new president on Friday have a clear message for the four candidates seeking election -- deal with the economy.

Rising prices and unemployment, especially amongst Iran's large young population, are common complaints of Tehran residents who will play a key role in deciding the successor to President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani after his two four-year terms allowed under the Iran's Islamic constitution.

Social issues, such as strict dress codes for women and education, and Iran's ties with the outside world are also in some voters' minds but for the majority they remain secondary to the pressing and everyday worry of high prices.

"Inflation has put heavy pressure on people who have fixed (government) salaries. Prices for housing, food and transport keep on going up. My salary does not," said a bank worker who took time-off with his wife and young son in a Tehran park.
Annual inflation, based on an index of commodities and services, has been tamed to an official figure of nearly 25 percent in the last Iranian year ending March 20, versus 50 percent in recent years.

Unemployment is officially put at 10 percent but this disguises underemployment and ignores the fact that some people take on at least a second or even third job to keep up with regular price hikes in this country of 60 million people, analysts said.

All four candidates in this week's election have weaved economic remedies into their public speeches and articles but given Iran is in the middle of a five-year plan (1995-2000) it is unclear how much room they would have for manoeuvre or what they would do with annual oil earnings of around $18 billion.

Tehran's large working-class and its growing middle-class, many of whom are on salaries or pensions fixed by the state, will be watching Rafsanjani's successor closely to see how he can help remedy the high cost of living.

"My pension is 230,000 rials a month ($77). Ten years ago half of this was enough but now even if it was doubled it would not cover my basic needs," said one retired health worker, who lives with his son and daughter-in-law to save money.
Inflation has also ravaged Tehran's housing and office space markets, making Tehran one of the world's most expensive cities to live for those with little foreign hard currency.
One couple who bought their city apartment for 70 million rials three years ago had seen the value of their flat quadruple while cars rarely devalue despite age and wear.
For men conscripted into military service on 20,000 rials a month, high prices mean that any entertainment on leave from barracks can be limited to strolling through landscaped parks.

One conscript who wanted to travel to his home-town which was shaken by a killer earthquake last week said he just could not afford to travel there since the cost of travel would eat up three-quarters of his monthly pay.

Even Tehran's middle-class, aided by the strong economic growth -- in the last Iranian year ending in March GDP grew by 4.5 percent -- feel the pinch of inflation and the lack of employment opportunities, especially for their children.
"My son has graduated from university as a chemist and my daughter is leaving high school. They cannot find work," said a middle-aged mother.

Alireza, a 30-year-old Tehran food shop owner, is frustrated by the high cost of rental accommodation and house prices while Farshid, a 20-year-old statistics university student, complains that text books are too expensive and he has little spare money to entertain his girlfriend.

The four candidates running in the election are former minister of culture and Islamic guidance Mohammad Khatami, parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, former internal security minister Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri and deputy head of the judiciary and only non-cleric in the contest Reza Zavarei.
